Deck cleaning in Melbourne

Timber is two materials in one board

Hard growth rings and soft growth between them. A pressure washer erodes the soft part and leaves the hard part standing, which is what furring is, and a furred deck holds dirt worse than it did before and feels rough underfoot. Decking is cleaned at low pressure, with the grain, or it is not cleaned at all.

  • Low pressure, always with the grain
  • Usually the step before oiling
  • Furring is permanent
Get A Quote 0400 638 010

What is actually on a grey deck

Three things, and they need different treatment. Biological growth, the black and green film that makes a deck slippery. Grey UV damage, which is the top layer of the timber itself breaking down in sunlight. And old coating, whatever oil or stain was last applied, now patchy.

Cleaning removes the first entirely and most of the third. It also removes the grey, because the degraded layer washes away and the sound timber underneath is the colour people are surprised by. What it cannot do is replace the coating, which is why a deck clean is normally the first half of a job and oiling is the second. A cleaned, bare deck left bare starts going grey again within months.

Why pressure is the wrong tool

The mechanism, in one section

STEP 01

The board is not uniform

Timber grows in rings. The dense dark bands are summer growth and the pale bands between them are spring growth, which is considerably softer.

STEP 02

Pressure finds the soft part

A high pressure jet erodes the spring growth faster than the summer growth, cutting shallow channels along the grain.

STEP 03

The deck furs

What is left is a ridged, fibrous surface. It feels rough, it catches bare feet, and it holds dirt in the new texture.

STEP 04

And it cannot be undone

Short of sanding the whole deck back, which is a different trade and a real cost. Which is why the pressure comes down and the chemistry does the work.

In a deck clean

Standard on timber work.

  • A timber-safe cleaning solution with dwell time, not just water
  • Low pressure, fan nozzle, always worked with the grain
  • Boards, risers, steps and the fascia around the deck
  • Balustrade, posts and handrails where they are timber
  • Gaps between boards cleared of leaf and debris
  • Neutralising rinse so no solution is left in the timber
  • An honest assessment of which boards are past cleaning

Not included

Related work that is a different trade or a second visit.

  • Oiling, staining or recoating, which has to happen on a dry deck days later
  • Sanding back a deck that has already been furred by pressure
  • Replacing rotten, split or cupped boards
  • Refixing loose boards, nails or protruding screws
  • Structural work on bearers, joists or posts
  • Composite and WPC decking, which is washed rather than treated as timber
  • Painted decks, where washing exposes failing paint rather than cleaning it

Questions

Asked about decking

Can my deck be cleaned without damaging it?

Yes, at the right pressure. What damages decking is a high pressure jet eroding the soft growth between the grain, and that is avoided by using a solution with dwell time and keeping the pressure low and the nozzle moving with the grain.

If your deck has already been furred by a previous clean, cleaning will not fix the texture. Sanding will, and that is a different trade.

My deck is grey. Will cleaning bring the colour back?

Usually, and often more than people expect. The grey is a degraded surface layer, and cleaning takes it off to reveal sound timber underneath. Boards that look written off frequently come up well.

It will go grey again if the deck is left bare, which is why cleaning and oiling are normally planned together.

Do you oil the deck afterwards?

We clean, we do not coat. Oiling has to happen on a thoroughly dry deck, which means days later, and it is a finishing trade with its own product decisions.

What we will do is tell you when the deck is dry enough and leave it in the right condition for whoever is applying the oil, which matters: oil over a deck that was not properly cleaned or neutralised does not bond.

How long before I can oil it?

Three to five clear days in a Melbourne summer and considerably longer through winter. Timber holds moisture far longer than it looks, and oil applied over a damp board traps it and fails.

A moisture meter is the reliable way to tell. Most decking oils want the timber below about fifteen percent.

Can you clean composite decking?

Yes, and it is a different job. Composite does not fur, but it does scar under pressure and some brands mark permanently, so it is washed with a solution and a soft brush rather than treated like timber.

It also grows mould in the grain texture just like timber does, which surprises people who bought it to avoid maintenance.

What about the timber screens and the pergola?

Same approach and worth doing at the same time, because they are usually in worse condition than the deck. Screens and battens are shaded on one face and that is where the growth is.
